title: Stick to the 18-Minute Rule
coreMove: Compress the talk until the central idea is stronger, not merely shorter.
sourcePressure: The source centers the eighteen-minute rule as a constraint that forces prioritization, serves the audience, protects attention, and reduces cognitive overload. The boundary is that shorter only helps when the main idea stays intact.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: The weak version says keep it short because attention spans are bad. The useful version says time pressure forces hierarchy, cuts drift, and preserves audience bandwidth.

sourceAnchors.name: 18-minute rule
sourceAnchors.detail: the source treats the eighteen-minute rule as a talk-length constraint that forces clearer prioritization and protects the audience from overload
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: The 18-minute rule is less a stopwatch trick than a demand to decide what the talk is truly carrying.

hook: speaker cuts slides the night before

exampleOpeningDiversity.rule: no more than 2 of the 6 examples may open with the pattern 'At HH:MM, <Name> <verb>s'
exampleOpeningDiversity.requiredOpenings: at least 4 distinct opening devices across the 6 examples, drawn from: timestamp+name+action, dialogue first line, sensory detail first, second-person 'You' direct address, retrospective 'It took her three weeks to see', question-as-hook, environmental detail before any human
exampleOpeningDiversity.rationale: C8 catches Cartesian repetition of phrases but not the deeper template of 'timestamp + named protagonist + prop + decision' that makes 6 examples feel like 1 example with name swaps

exampleSpecs.audience: a theatre director with twenty minutes to defend a community program
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether extra background buries the one proof that the program changes attendance
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: she lays every story card on the floor, keeps the three that prove the program's effect, and cuts the history section before rehearsal
exampleSpecs.firstImage: index cards spread across a black-box theatre floor

exampleSpecs.audience: a public-health doctor briefing parents before a school clinic
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether parents keep the essential risk and consent points without overload
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: he compares a twelve-point draft with three parent questions from last year's clinic and rebuilds the briefing around those questions only
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a consent form clipped under a stopwatch on a cafeteria table

exampleSpecs.audience: a junior attorney preparing a closing argument for a small civil trial
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether jurors remember the central breach or drown in every email
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: she removes seven emails from the binder and keeps the one timeline jurors can hold in working memory
exampleSpecs.firstImage: paper clips snapping off a thick binder of printed emails

exampleSpecs.audience: a director introducing a new gallery to members and local press
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether the audience leaves with one curatorial idea instead of a full donor list
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: after a board member asks to thank twelve more people, he protects the two-minute object story and moves extra acknowledgments to the printed program
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a printed program folded beside a velvet gallery rope

exampleSpecs.audience: a product lead presenting a roadmap to customer-support managers
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether the room understands the tradeoff behind one delayed feature
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: he asks which feature will reduce support tickets fastest, then cuts the platform tour and spends the saved minutes on the tradeoff slide
exampleSpecs.firstImage: colored roadmap bars compressed on a wall monitor

exampleSpecs.audience: an emergency manager updating residents after a river flood
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether worried residents hear the next three decisions instead of every agency detail
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: you watch him cut the agency roster, keep the shelter, debris, and permit sequence, and use the final minute for where residents go next
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a damp folding chair facing a gymnasium stage

skillTargets: choose what to cut based on the main idea
analyze audience cognitive load in a talk plan
evaluate whether brevity protects substance or weakens it

tryThisNowSpec: Write the one sentence your audience must still remember tomorrow, then circle every slide, story, or detail that does not make that sentence easier to keep.

rhythmVariety.deepReadParagraphLengthMix: at least one paragraph 3 sentences or shorter, at least one paragraph 5+ sentences, at least one one-sentence punch line
rhythmVariety.fullReadInterludeRequirement: at least one paragraph that breaks the scene-then-rule rhythm: a question to the reader, a research aside, a direct second-person passage, or a brief historical reference
rhythmVariety.forbiddenRhythm: every paragraph following the pattern 'concrete anchor sentence -> abstract rule sentence -> elaboration sentence'
